lessons.title: Pediatric trauma: small bodies, different rules
lessons.body:
## Same energy, smaller target

A child hit by a car absorbs the same kinetic energy an adult would, spread across a body with less fat, less muscle, and organs packed closer together. Energy that would snap one adult bone travels through a child and injures several systems at once. **Multisystem injury is the expectation in a hurt child, not the exception.**

A child's ribs are still partly cartilage and bend instead of breaking. The lung underneath can be badly bruised behind a perfectly normal chest wall, so **no rib fractures does not mean no chest injury**. The reverse is also true: rib fractures in a small child took enormous force, and in an infant they raise the question of inflicted injury.

The liver and spleen sit lower and are less covered by the rib cage, which is why handlebar and lap-belt injuries hit them directly.

## Head heavy, short necked

The head is about `18%` of body surface in an infant against `9%` in an adult, and it leads in every fall. Expect head injury first. That large occiput also shoves the neck into flexion when a small child lies flat, so **pad from the shoulders to the hips** to bring the airway back to neutral. The tongue is large for the mouth and the airway is narrow, so a small amount of swelling closes it.

## Numbers that change with age

| Age | Heart rate | Respiratory rate | Systolic floor |
|---|---|---|---|
| Infant under 1 | `100–160` | `30–60` | `70` |
| Toddler 1–3 | `90–150` | `24–40` | `72–76` |
| Preschool 4–5 | `80–140` | `22–34` | `78–80` |
| School age 6–12 | `70–120` | `18–30` | `82–94` |
| Adolescent 13+ | `60–100` | `12–20` | `90` |

Past the first year the systolic floor is roughly `70 + (2 × age in years)`. Below that number the child is hypotensive, and a hypotensive child has usually already lost `30–45%` of blood volume.

Total blood volume is about `70–80 mL/kg`. A `20 kg` five-year-old holds roughly `1.5 L`, so a scalp laceration that is a nuisance in an adult can be a class II hemorrhage in a preschooler. Infants can bleed enough into a scalp hematoma alone to go into shock.

> **Key:** Children hold their blood pressure until they cannot, then crash without a warning slide. Judge a hurt child on heart rate, skin color, capillary refill, and whether they interact with you. Tachycardia is the earliest reliable sign of shock in a child.

## The first ten seconds

The **pediatric assessment triangle** is appearance, work of breathing, and circulation to skin, read from the doorway before you touch anyone. A child who will not look at you, will not cry, will not reach for a parent, or does not fight your exam is sick until proven otherwise.

## Heat, pain, and parents

High surface area and thin skin mean children cool fast, and cold children stop clotting. Cover the head, turn up the patient compartment, and expose only as much as you need to. Keep a parent where the child can see them; a calm parent drops a heart rate better than anything in your bag.

## When the story does not fit

Injuries that do not match the stated mechanism, a delay in calling, a story that changes between tellings, bruising on the torso, ears, or neck of a child under `4`, any bruise on an infant who is not yet crawling or cruising, patterned burns, and rib fractures in an infant all raise concern for inflicted injury. New Jersey EMTs are mandatory reporters. Write what you saw and what you were told, word for word, treat the injuries, and report it. Investigating is not your job.

> **On the exam:** A child with a normal blood pressure, a heart rate well above the range for age, and delayed capillary refill is in compensated shock. The answer is never to wait and reassess.
keyPoints: Flexible pediatric ribs mean serious lung contusion with no fracture; rib fractures in a small child mean enormous force.
An infant head is about 18 percent of body surface, so pad from shoulders to hips to hold a small child's airway neutral.
Systolic floor past age 1 is about 70 plus 2 times age in years, and hypotension means 30 to 45 percent of volume is gone.
Blood volume is 70 to 80 mL/kg, so a 20 kg child holds roughly 1.5 liters and scalp bleeding can cause shock.
Tachycardia, skin signs, capillary refill and interaction are the pediatric shock signs, not blood pressure.

checks.q: A 6-year-old struck by a car has a blood pressure of 88/54, a heart rate of 158, and capillary refill of 4 seconds. How should you read this?
choices: Normal findings for his age; continue the assessment without changing priorities
Compensated shock, because the pressure is still above the floor for age but perfusion is not keeping up
Decompensated shock requiring immediate defibrillation
Neurogenic shock from an unrecognized spinal injury
checks.why: The systolic floor for a 6-year-old is about 70 plus 12, or 82, so 88 is technically above it. The tachycardia and 4-second refill are the compensation. A child in this state is one adrenaline reserve away from crashing, so the response is rapid transport, warmth and reassessment, not waiting.

checks.q: Why do you pad from the shoulders to the hips when securing a 2-year-old on a flat surface?
choices: The large occiput flexes the neck forward and narrows the airway
It keeps the child from sliding off the device during transport
It raises the legs and improves venous return
It prevents pressure sores over the sacrum
checks.why: A small child's head is disproportionately large, so lying flat pushes the chin toward the chest. Padding under the torso lifts the body to match the head and restores a neutral airway. Pressure sores and sliding are real problems but are not why the padding goes there.

checks.q: What is the approximate systolic blood pressure floor for a 5-year-old?
choices: 60 mmHg
95 mmHg
70 mmHg
80 mmHg
checks.why: The formula is 70 plus 2 times the age in years, so 70 plus 10 equals 80 mmHg. Anything below that is hypotension in a 5-year-old and signals that roughly a third or more of blood volume is already lost.

lessons.title: Geriatric trauma and the anticoagulated patient
lessons.body:
## Old vessels lie to you

Maximum heart rate falls with age, roughly `220` minus the age in years, and a large share of older patients take a beta blocker or a rate-controlling calcium channel blocker. The tachycardia you depend on to spot shock may simply never show up.

Arteries stiffen, so baseline blood pressure drifts upward. A patient who lives at `170/90` and hands you `118/70` has lost a third of his pressure while the monitor prints a number that looks fine. Ask the family what his pressure usually runs, or read the medication list, and treat any normal-looking pressure in an injured older adult with suspicion.

Kidneys, lungs and immune function all carry less reserve, so the margin between under-resuscitated and fluid-overloaded is narrow.

## Bones and brains that give way early

Bone density falls after about age `50`, faster in women after menopause. A ground-level fall — the most common geriatric mechanism by far — produces hip fractures, distal radius fractures and vertebral compression fractures at forces that would not bruise a 25-year-old.

Rib fractures deserve their own alarm. In patients over `65`, each additional fractured rib raises mortality and pneumonia risk, because pain produces shallow breathing, which collapses alveoli and invites infection. Three or more rib fractures in an older adult is a trauma-center problem.

The brain shrinks with age, which stretches the bridging veins running from brain to skull and leaves empty space for blood to collect before any pressure sign appears. That is why an older patient can carry a sizeable **subdural hematoma** with a normal exam and deteriorate days later.

In the neck, arthritic narrowing plus a hyperextension fall onto the face produces **central cord syndrome**: weakness that is worse in the hands and arms than in the legs, often with burning pain, and frequently with no fracture at all.

## Blood thinners change the arithmetic

Ask by drug name and write it down.

| Drug | Type | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Warfarin | Vitamin K antagonist | Reversed with vitamin K plus clotting factor concentrate; ask about the INR |
| Apixaban, rivaroxaban | Factor Xa inhibitor | Reversed with andexanet alfa or factor concentrate; no routine blood test |
| Dabigatran | Direct thrombin inhibitor | Reversed with idarucizumab |
| Clopidogrel, ticagrelor, aspirin | Antiplatelet | No true reversal agent exists |

Any head strike on any of these earns imaging and usually a period of observation even with a normal exam, because the bleed can be delayed by hours. The national field triage guideline treats anticoagulant use with head injury as a reason to consider a trauma center, and lists age over `65` as a special consideration in its own right.

> **Key:** In an older trauma patient a normal heart rate and a normal blood pressure are not reassurance. Ask what those numbers usually are and which medications are holding them there.

## Handling them without hurting them

Kyphosis means the head will not reach a flat surface. **Fill the gap with padding rather than pressing the head down** — forcing that curve straight can injure the cord. Size a collar carefully, and where none fits the curve, use towel rolls and head blocks instead.

Skin is paper thin and tears under tape, so favor roller gauze and soft dressings. Warm them early; older patients lose heat quickly and arrive hypothermic from a `60°F` living room.

Get a baseline mental status from somebody who knows the patient. Confusion may be two years old or two hours old, and only a family member can tell you which.

> **On shift:** Older trauma patients are under-triaged more than any other group. The mechanism looks trivial, the numbers look fine, and the injury is severe. A fall from standing in a patient on a blood thinner deserves the same seriousness as a car crash.
keyPoints: Beta blockers and a lower maximum heart rate remove the tachycardia you use to detect shock in older patients.
Stiff arteries raise baseline pressure, so a normal-looking 118/70 may be profound hypotension for someone who lives at 170/90.
Brain shrinkage stretches bridging veins, so subdural hematomas occur after trivial mechanisms and can present days later.
Any head strike on warfarin, a factor Xa inhibitor, dabigatran or an antiplatelet earns imaging and observation even with a normal exam.
Pad the gap created by kyphosis instead of forcing the head flat, and protect fragile skin from tape.

checks.q: An 80-year-old on metoprolol fell down four stairs. He is pale and diaphoretic with a heart rate of 82 and a blood pressure of 110/78. His daughter says he normally runs 165/85. What is the most likely interpretation?
choices: He is stable, since both numbers fall within adult normal ranges
He is in shock, with the beta blocker blocking the tachycardia and the pressure already down substantially from his baseline
He has neurogenic shock from a cervical fracture
The blood pressure cuff is reading falsely low because of arterial stiffness
checks.why: Pale and diaphoretic skin is a perfusion finding and outranks the numbers. Metoprolol prevents the compensatory tachycardia, and a drop from 165 to 110 systolic is a loss of about a third of his usual pressure. Neurogenic shock gives warm dry skin with bradycardia, which does not fit.

checks.q: Which anticoagulant has a specific reversal agent called idarucizumab?
choices: Warfarin
Clopidogrel
Dabigatran
Apixaban
checks.why: Idarucizumab reverses dabigatran, a direct thrombin inhibitor. Warfarin is reversed with vitamin K and factor concentrate, apixaban with andexanet alfa or factor concentrate, and clopidogrel has no true reversal agent. Naming the exact drug at handoff shortens the time to reversal.

checks.q: An 88-year-old with a pronounced kyphotic curve cannot lie flat, and her head hangs several inches above the stretcher mattress. What should you do?
choices: Fill the space behind her head and neck with padding and secure her in her natural position
Apply firm downward pressure to bring the head flat, then apply a collar
Transport her sitting fully upright without any head support
Use a rigid long board so the straps can pull the spine into alignment
checks.why: Forcing a fused kyphotic spine straight can injure the cord and is painful and useless. Padding the gap immobilizes her in the position her spine already lives in. Sitting fully upright with no support leaves the head free to move, and strapping a curved spine to a flat board does exactly the harm you are trying to prevent.

lessons.title: Trauma in pregnancy: two patients, one circulation
lessons.body:
## The numbers move before the pregnancy shows

Trauma is the leading non-obstetric cause of maternal death, and the usual sources are motor vehicle crashes, falls and intimate partner violence. Screening quietly for the last one is part of the assessment.

By the third trimester blood volume is up `40–50%` and the resting heart rate runs `10–20` beats faster than her baseline. Blood pressure typically falls `10–15 mmHg` during the second trimester and drifts back toward normal near term. Put those together and a pregnant patient can lose `1200–1500 mL` of blood before her vital signs move at all.

Worse, the body defends itself by clamping down on the uterine circulation first. **Fetal distress appears before maternal vital signs change**, so a normal maternal blood pressure tells you nothing about the fetus.

## Supine hypotensive syndrome

After about `20 weeks` the uterus is heavy enough to compress the inferior vena cava when she lies flat. Venous return falls and cardiac output can drop by up to `30%` within minutes. She goes pale, sweaty, nauseated and hypotensive on your stretcher for no other reason.

Fix it by tilting the stretcher or the board `15–30 degrees` to the **left**. If she must stay flat, reach across and **manually displace the uterus to the left** with both hands and hold it there. Manual displacement works at least as well as tilting and leaves the chest flat for compressions.

## Dating the pregnancy without a chart

Fundal height gives you a usable estimate: at the pubic symphysis is about `12 weeks`, at the umbilicus about `20 weeks`, and roughly `1 cm` above the symphysis per week after that. Twenty weeks is where left tilt, fetal concern and the pregnancy triage criterion all begin.

## What actually harms the fetus

**Placental abruption**, the placenta shearing off the uterine wall, is the leading cause of fetal death when the mother survives. Deceleration causes it, so it follows crashes and falls that look survivable. Look for abdominal pain, a firm, rigid or tender uterus, contractions, and vaginal bleeding — which is often **concealed** behind the placenta and never appears outside.

It can declare itself hours later. That is why **every pregnant patient past 20 weeks is transported after any trauma**, including a low-speed crash with no complaints. Standard care is `4–6 hours` of fetal heart and contraction monitoring.

**Uterine rupture** is rare and catastrophic: severe pain, loss of the normal uterine contour, easily palpable fetal parts and shock.

Direct fetal injury is uncommon because amniotic fluid cushions well; the exception is a late-term fetal skull fracture when the head is already down in the pelvis.

## Belts, questions and blood type

The lap belt belongs **low across the hips and under the belly**, with the shoulder belt between the breasts and off to the side of the uterus. A belt riding across the uterus transmits force straight into the placenta. Airbags are not contraindicated in pregnancy.

Ask: how many weeks, how many prior pregnancies, any bleeding or fluid, is the baby moving, any contractions, and what her blood type is. An **Rh-negative** mother needs Rh immune globulin after even minor abdominal trauma.

> **Key:** The best care for the fetus is resuscitation of the mother. Oxygen generously, control bleeding aggressively, tilt or displace left, and transport to a facility with obstetric capability.

## If she arrests

CPR continues with **continuous manual left uterine displacement**, with standard hand placement on the lower half of the sternum. The hospital target for a resuscitative hysterotomy, delivering the fetus to unload the vena cava and improve the mother's circulation, is about `4–5 minutes` into the arrest. That deadline makes early notification and a short scene time the interventions that belong to you.

> **Trap:** A reassuring blood pressure does not end the assessment. The pregnant patient who feels fine after a fender-bender still goes, because abruption is silent right up until it is not.
keyPoints: Blood volume rises 40 to 50 percent, so a pregnant patient can lose 1200 to 1500 mL before her vital signs change.
The uterus is sacrificed first, so fetal distress precedes any change in maternal vitals.
Past 20 weeks, tilt the stretcher 15 to 30 degrees left or manually displace the uterus to the left to keep it off the vena cava.
Placental abruption is the leading cause of fetal death in a surviving mother, its bleeding is often concealed, and it can appear hours later.
Every pregnant patient past 20 weeks is transported after any trauma, and Rh-negative mothers need Rh immune globulin.

checks.q: A 33-week pregnant woman was a restrained driver in a 25 mph crash. She has no pain, normal vital signs and no vaginal bleeding, and wants to go home. What is the correct advice?
choices: She may sign a refusal since she is asymptomatic with a low-speed mechanism
She should be transported, because placental abruption can be concealed and can present hours later
She needs transport only if fetal movement has decreased
She should follow up with her obstetrician in the next few days
checks.why: Abruption follows deceleration, can bleed entirely behind the placenta with no external blood, and can declare hours after the event. Standard care past 20 weeks is transport and 4 to 6 hours of fetal monitoring. Waiting for decreased movement or an office visit lets a treatable abruption become a fetal death.

checks.q: A 28-week pregnant trauma patient becomes pale and hypotensive within two minutes of being laid supine on the backboard. What is the first correction?
choices: Raise her legs to improve venous return
Sit her fully upright and remove spinal precautions
Tilt the board 15 to 30 degrees to the left or manually displace the uterus to the left
Give a nitroglycerin tablet for the pressure change
checks.why: This is supine hypotensive syndrome from the uterus compressing the inferior vena cava, and the fix is mechanical. Left tilt or manual left uterine displacement restores venous return immediately. Raising the legs does not unload the cava, abandoning spinal precautions is not indicated by the hypotension, and nitroglycerin would make it worse.

checks.q: You palpate the fundus at the level of the umbilicus. What is the approximate gestational age?
choices: About 12 weeks
About 20 weeks
About 30 weeks
About 36 weeks
checks.why: The fundus reaches the pubic symphysis around 12 weeks and the umbilicus around 20 weeks, then climbs roughly 1 cm per week. Twenty weeks is the threshold for left tilt, for fetal monitoring, and for counting pregnancy as a special field triage consideration.

lessons.title: Penetrating wounds of the chest and abdomen
lessons.body:
## Count the holes, then count them again

A penetrating patient is a geometry problem. What matters is where the track went, not how the skin looks. Fully expose and look in the places wounds hide: the back, the axilla, the groin and perineum, the scalp, under skin folds, and between the buttocks. An **odd number of holes** in a gunshot patient means something is still inside.

Do not probe, sound or irrigate a wound to trace the path. You will start bleeding that had stopped and you will learn nothing the operating room will not learn better.

## Two maps worth memorizing

The **cardiac box** runs between the nipples, from the sternal notch down to the costal margin. A penetrating wound in that rectangle threatens the heart and great vessels, so tamponade is on the list from the first second.

The **thoracoabdominal zone** runs from the nipple line in front (the fourth intercostal space) and the tip of the scapula in back down to the costal margins. The diaphragm rises as high as the fourth intercostal space on a full exhalation, so anything entering that band may have crossed it. **A wound there is a chest injury and a belly injury until surgery says otherwise.**

The neck is divided into three zones: **zone I** from the clavicles to the cricoid cartilage, with the great vessels and the top of the chest; **zone II** from the cricoid to the angle of the jaw, the most exposed and most commonly injured; **zone III** above the angle of the jaw to the base of the skull, difficult to reach surgically.

## Hard signs that mean move now

- Expanding or pulsatile hematoma
- Severe active external bleeding
- A bruit or a palpable thrill over the wound
- Absent or clearly diminished distal pulse
- Airway compromise, stridor, or a rapidly enlarging neck
- Massive coughing or vomiting of blood

Any one of these is a surgical emergency. Note it out loud and start moving.

## What you do to each region

**Neck.** Cover an open neck wound with an **occlusive dressing** to prevent air from being sucked into an injured vein, which causes air embolism. Apply direct pressure over the vessel, never circumferentially around the neck, and never wrap both sides at once. Keep suction at hand.

**Chest.** Vented chest seal or a dressing taped on three sides, high-flow oxygen, and reassess breath sounds every few minutes. Roll the patient once and seal the exit wound too. If they deteriorate after sealing, burp the seal.

**Abdomen.** Assume both a bleeding solid organ and a leaking hollow organ, plus the retroperitoneum that you can neither see nor examine. A soft abdomen proves nothing early. Cover the wound, do not palpate repeatedly, nothing by mouth, and go.

**Impaled objects** stay in place, stabilized, unless they block the airway or CPR.

> **Key:** Penetrating torso trauma is a load-and-go. Scene time under `10 minutes`, ideally under `5`. The intervention that saves this patient is a surgeon, and everything you do on scene that is not airway or gross hemorrhage control is delay.

## Spinal precautions and penetrating trauma

Routine spinal motion restriction is **not** indicated for isolated penetrating trauma without a neurologic deficit. Collars hide expanding neck hematomas, boards add minutes, and the evidence shows worse outcomes. If there is a deficit, restrict.

## What the trauma team will ask

Weapon type, and caliber if anyone knows it. How many shots were heard. Distance from the shooter. For stabbings, the blade length and the angle. Time of injury. Whether the patient walked or was carried. Get it at the scene from police or bystanders, because in ten minutes nobody will be there to ask.

> **On the exam:** A stab wound below the nipple line is asked about as an abdominal injury even though the hole is on the chest. The diaphragm is the reason.
keyPoints: Expose fully and count wounds; an odd number of holes in a gunshot patient means retained projectile.
The cardiac box lies between the nipples from sternal notch to costal margin and puts tamponade on your list.
The thoracoabdominal zone runs from the nipple line down to the costal margins, and wounds there are both chest and belly injuries.
Open neck wounds get an occlusive dressing to prevent air embolism and pressure over the vessel, never circumferential wrapping.
Penetrating torso trauma is load-and-go, and routine spinal motion restriction is not indicated without a neurologic deficit.

checks.q: A man is stabbed once just below the left nipple. He is alert with clear lung sounds and a soft abdomen. How should you classify the injury?
choices: An isolated chest wound, since the abdomen is soft
A superficial wound, since he is alert with normal lung sounds
A potential chest and abdominal injury, because the diaphragm rises to the fourth intercostal space on exhalation
An abdominal wound only, because the blade must have travelled downward
checks.why: The nipple line marks the top of the thoracoabdominal zone. On full exhalation the diaphragm climbs to about the fourth intercostal space, so a blade entering there can be in the chest, the abdomen, or both. A soft abdomen early means nothing, and normal lung sounds do not exclude a diaphragm or liver injury.

checks.q: Which finding is a hard sign of vascular injury that demands immediate transport?
choices: A small non-expanding hematoma around the wound
An expanding pulsatile hematoma with a palpable thrill
Mild tenderness at the wound edges
A wound that stopped bleeding after direct pressure
checks.why: Expanding or pulsatile hematoma, thrill or bruit, severe bleeding, absent distal pulse and airway compromise are the hard signs and all mean a surgeon now. A small stable hematoma, local tenderness and bleeding that stopped with pressure are soft findings that still get evaluated but do not by themselves define a vascular emergency.

checks.q: A patient has an isolated gunshot wound to the left thigh. He is alert, moves all extremities and has no neck or back pain. What spinal care is indicated?
choices: None; routine spinal motion restriction is not indicated for isolated penetrating trauma without a deficit
Full collar and long board because any gunshot is a significant mechanism
Collar only, without a board
Manual in-line stabilization for the entire transport
checks.why: Immobilizing penetrating trauma patients without neurologic deficit delays surgery and is associated with worse outcomes. The device also hides expanding hematomas. If he had weakness, numbness or a deficit, restriction would be appropriate, but a bullet in the thigh with an intact neurologic exam does not earn a board.

lessons.title: Crush syndrome and blast injury up close
lessons.body:
## What dying muscle does

Compressed muscle loses its blood supply. Cell membranes fail, and the cell contents spill into the space around them: **potassium**, phosphate, **myoglobin**, uric acid and lactic acid. While the weight is still on, all of that stays trapped locally and the patient may look and sound fine.

At the same time fluid pours out of the circulation into the crushed tissue. A badly crushed limb can third-space `10–12 L` over `48 hours`, so the patient is already hypovolemic before anything is lifted.

## The moment of release

Lift the load and the trapped load washes in.

- **Hyperkalemia** hits the heart within minutes: peaked T waves, then a widening QRS, then a sine wave, then ventricular fibrillation or asystole.
- **Myoglobin** clogs the kidney tubules and causes acute kidney injury; the urine turns tea-colored or cola-colored.
- **Metabolic acidosis** from lactic acid worsens the rhythm problem and the clotting problem.
- **Hypocalcemia** develops as calcium is dragged into damaged muscle.

Rescuers have named this the smiling death: a patient who is talking to you under the rubble arrests minutes after the concrete comes off. After roughly `1 hour` of compression, assume crush syndrome is possible; after `4 hours` assume it is likely.

> **Key:** Prepare before you lift. ALS on scene, monitor on the chest, vascular access established and fluid running **before** the weight comes off. Typical prehospital practice is isotonic fluid started pre-release and continued at a high rate, with calcium, sodium bicarbonate and nebulized albuterol available as potassium-shifting measures. None of those are EMT interventions, which is exactly why the EMT's job is to call early and to say the word entrapment on the radio.

Your own tasks are real: note and report the **time entrapment began**, keep the patient warm, keep the airway open, give oxygen, and do not let anyone move the object until the team says go. Field amputation exists, is extremely rare, and is a physician decision.

After release, watch the limb for **compartment syndrome** over the next `6–8 hours`: pain far out of proportion, pain on passive stretch, tightness, numbness. The pulse stays present until very late.

## Blast physics

An explosion creates a pressure wave that travels faster than sound and then a blast wind behind it. Four injury mechanisms, and one patient routinely has several.

1. **Primary**, from the overpressure itself, injuring air-filled organs.
2. **Secondary**, from flying fragments. The most common cause of injury and death.
3. **Tertiary**, from the body being thrown into something.
4. **Quaternary**, everything else: burns, inhaled toxins, crush from a collapse, carbon monoxide, and worsening of existing disease such as asthma.

Primary injury follows thresholds. Eardrums rupture around `5 psi` of overpressure, and **a ruptured eardrum is not a reliable screen for blast lung** — plenty of patients have one without the other in each direction. Lung injury generally needs `15–40 psi`. Bowel injury is even higher and may declare itself a day later as perforation.

**Enclosed spaces and underwater blasts multiply the overpressure**, because the wave reflects instead of dissipating. The same device that bruises someone in a parking lot kills someone in a bus.

## Blast lung

The classic picture is dyspnea, hypoxia, chest pain and coughing up blood, sometimes with the triad of apnea, bradycardia and hypotension right after the event. It can take hours to appear, so a walking, talking blast patient still needs lungs rechecked on the way in.

Give high-flow oxygen. Be careful with positive pressure: forcing air into damaged lung can cause a pneumothorax or push air into a torn vessel as an **arterial gas embolism**. If a blast patient suddenly deteriorates after you start bagging, think tension pneumothorax or air embolism, not a failed seal.

> **Trap:** Secondary devices are timed for responders. Do not park in the obvious approach lane, do not cluster, do not touch unattended bags, and move patients away from the structure before you work on them.
keyPoints: Crushed muscle spills potassium, myoglobin and acid, which stay trapped until the weight is lifted.
On release, hyperkalemia causes peaked T waves, a widening QRS and arrest, and myoglobin causes kidney injury.
Prepare before lifting: ALS, monitor, and fluid running pre-release; the EMT's job is to call early and note the entrapment start time.
Blast injury has four mechanisms, and enclosed or underwater blasts multiply the overpressure.
Eardrum rupture does not reliably predict blast lung, and positive pressure in a blast patient can cause pneumothorax or air embolism.

checks.q: A worker has been pinned under a machine for 3 hours. He is alert and conversational. Fire says they can lift it in 2 minutes. What is the most important action?
choices: Lift immediately, since he is alert and every minute of compression adds injury
Hold the lift until ALS has a monitor on and fluid running, then coordinate the release
Apply a tourniquet above the crushed area and then lift
Give oral fluids to correct his dehydration before the lift
checks.why: He looks well precisely because the toxins are still trapped. Three hours of compression makes crush syndrome likely, and the arrest happens at release. The preparation is monitoring, access and fluid before the weight moves. A tourniquet is not a routine answer here, and oral fluids do nothing for hyperkalemia and risk aspiration.

checks.q: Which finding is the earliest cardiac sign of the hyperkalemia that follows a crush release?
choices: ST elevation in the inferior leads
A prolonged QT interval
Peaked T waves
Atrial fibrillation with a rapid ventricular response
checks.why: Rising potassium produces peaked T waves first, then a widening QRS, then a sine-wave pattern, then ventricular fibrillation or asystole. ST elevation is ischemia, QT prolongation is more typical of low potassium or drug effect, and atrial fibrillation is not the hyperkalemia pattern.

checks.q: A man standing 20 feet from a bomb that detonated inside a small restaurant is walking, talking, and has only minor cuts. What is the correct concern?
choices: He is uninjured because he has no visible chest wound
An enclosed-space blast multiplies overpressure, so blast lung can appear over the next few hours
He needs no reassessment as long as his eardrums are intact
His only realistic risk is delayed infection from the lacerations
checks.why: Reflected pressure waves in a confined space produce far higher overpressure than the same device outdoors. Blast lung can take hours to declare, so reassess breathing and oxygen saturation en route. Intact eardrums do not rule out lung injury, and treating him as uninjured because the skin looks fine is the classic blast mistake.

lessons.title: Tourniquets second pass: conversion, myths, and TXA
lessons.body:
## What the data actually says

Military and civilian series point the same direction: tourniquets applied **before** the patient goes into shock are associated with far better survival, and limb loss caused by the tourniquet itself is rare. Routine safe time is about `2 hours`, and limbs have been salvaged after `6 hours` on a properly applied device. The limb is almost never what kills; the bleeding is.

## Five myths worth killing

1. **A tourniquet costs the limb.** It usually does not. The wound that made you reach for it is the threat to the limb.
2. **Loosen it every fifteen or twenty minutes.** Never. Intermittent release restarts the bleeding and washes acid and potassium into the circulation repeatedly, which is the worst of both worlds.
3. **It is a last resort.** It is **first-line** for life-threatening limb bleeding, and immediate for an amputation, a spurting arterial wound, or a patient whose airway you must also manage.
4. **The bleeding has to be spurting and arterial.** Venous or mixed limb bleeding that will not stop with pressure qualifies.
5. **Anything narrow will do in a pinch.** A strap at least `1.5 in` wide spreads the pressure. Belts, cords and wire are narrow, hard to tension, and often fail to occlude arterial flow while still obstructing venous return, which makes bleeding worse.

## Why a tourniquet fails

The most common failure is simply **not tight enough**. If the wound is still bleeding or a distal pulse is still present, tighten further or place a **second tourniquet directly above the first**. Other failures: placed over a joint, placed too close to the wound on a mangled segment, windlass not clipped and secured, applied over a bulging cargo pocket, or applied to a large thigh where one device cannot generate enough pressure.

Place it **high and tight over clothing** when you cannot see the wound or the scene is unsafe, and place it deliberately `2–3 in` above the wound once you can work. Write the **time** on the device.

## Conversion

Conversion means replacing a tourniquet with wound packing and a pressure dressing so blood flow returns to the limb. It is a protocol-driven decision and rarely applies to a short urban transport. Where protocols permit it, the general criteria are all of these:

- Less than about `2 hours` since application
- The patient is not in shock
- The bleeding can plausibly be controlled by packing and pressure
- It is not a complete or near-complete amputation, and not a mangled limb
- You can watch the wound continuously and have the ability to retighten
- Transport is long enough that the limb benefits

The technique: pack the wound and apply a firm pressure dressing first, then **loosen the windlass slowly without removing the device**, watch for a full `2 minutes`, and leave the loosened tourniquet in place ready to be retightened. If bleeding restarts, retighten and do not try again.

> **Trap:** Never convert a tourniquet that has been in place more than about `6 hours`, and never convert during a short transport just because the patient is uncomfortable. Pain is not a conversion criterion.

## Junctions

Groin, armpit and neck cannot be tourniqueted. Those get **hemostatic gauze packed to the depth of the bleeding vessel** and `3 minutes` of firm held pressure. Purpose-built junctional tourniquets exist where a service carries them.

## Tranexamic acid

TXA is an antifibrinolytic. Clots break down through a process that begins with plasminogen binding to fibrin; TXA occupies that binding site, so clots that have formed are not dissolved prematurely. It does not create clot. It protects the clot you or the body made.

- The dose in most systems is `1 g` intravenously over `10 minutes`, followed by `1 g` over `8 hours`, though some services give a `2 g` bolus.
- The benefit is **time-dependent**: greatest within `1 hour` of injury, still present out to `3 hours`, and after `3 hours` it may cause harm.
- It is an ALS or hospital medication in most systems, outside EMT scope.

> **Key:** The EMT contribution to TXA is the **time of injury**, documented and handed off. Without that number the three-hour window cannot be used, and the drug cannot be given safely.

> **On shift:** TXA never replaces pressure, packing or a tourniquet. Mechanical control first; the drug only keeps the clot you achieved from falling apart.
keyPoints: Tourniquets are first-line for life-threatening limb bleeding; routine safe time is about 2 hours and limbs have survived 6.
Never loosen a tourniquet periodically, and the most common failure is that it is not tight enough.
Conversion requires under 2 hours, no shock, controllable bleeding, no amputation, continuous observation and a long transport, and pain is not a criterion.
Junctional wounds get hemostatic gauze packed to the vessel and 3 minutes of held pressure.
TXA is 1 g IV over 10 minutes, works best within 1 hour and may harm after 3, so the documented time of injury is the EMT's contribution.

checks.q: You applied a tourniquet 15 minutes ago. The wound has stopped bleeding but you can still feel a weak radial pulse distal to it. What should you do?
choices: Nothing; the bleeding is controlled, which is the goal
Tighten further, or add a second tourniquet directly above the first, until the distal pulse is gone
Loosen and reapply lower on the limb
Remove it and apply a pressure dressing instead
checks.why: A persistent distal pulse means arterial inflow is continuing while venous outflow is blocked, which can increase bleeding and cause compartment problems. The endpoint is bleeding stopped and distal pulse absent. Loosening, moving it lower or removing it all restart the bleeding.

checks.q: Which patient is the worst candidate for tourniquet conversion?
choices: A stable patient with a controlled thigh laceration, tourniquet on 40 minutes, with a 90-minute transport ahead
A patient with a near-complete forearm amputation who is tachycardic and pale
A stable patient with a calf wound that packed easily, tourniquet on 30 minutes
A stable patient with a controlled arm wound and continuous monitoring available
checks.why: Shock and an amputation or mangled limb are both absolute reasons not to convert. Conversion is considered only in a stable patient, under roughly 2 hours, with bleeding that packing can hold and a transport long enough to matter. The other three meet those conditions.

checks.q: Why does the documented time of injury matter for tranexamic acid?
choices: TXA dissolves existing clots, so it must be given before clots form
TXA works best within 1 hour, is still useful to 3 hours, and may cause harm after 3 hours
TXA must be given exactly 3 hours after injury to be effective
The dose changes every hour after injury
checks.why: TXA is an antifibrinolytic that protects clot rather than dissolving it, and its benefit is strongly time dependent. Given within an hour it saves the most lives, out to three hours it still helps, and beyond three hours the data suggests possible harm. The dose does not change hourly.

lessons.title: The pelvic binder, step by step
lessons.body:
## Why closing a ring stops bleeding

The pelvis is a ring of bone. A ring can only break in at least two places, which is why a single obvious fracture usually means a second injury on the other side. Inside and around that ring sit a dense web of veins, the arteries feeding the pelvis, and a large potential space that can hold `2 L` or more of blood without looking distended from the outside.

Most pelvic bleeding — roughly `80–90%` of it — is **venous and from the broken bone surfaces**, not from a single named artery. That matters because venous bleeding stops when the space stops expanding. Closing the ring reduces the volume available to fill, brings the bone ends back into contact, and lets pressure build enough to tamponade. A binder is a bleeding control device, not a comfort device.

## Three patterns

- **Anteroposterior compression**, the open book: the front of the ring springs apart, often from a head-on crash or a crush from front to back. This is the pattern a binder helps most.
- **Lateral compression**: force from the side drives one half inward. A binder still helps, but over-tightening can push the fragments further in.
- **Vertical shear**: a fall from height drives one half of the pelvis upward. Highly unstable.

## Who gets one

Apply a binder for any of these:

- Significant mechanism plus pelvic pain, tenderness, or instability
- Unexplained shock with a mechanism that could break the pelvis
- An unresponsive patient with a significant mechanism who cannot be examined
- Obvious deformity, leg length difference, or a leg rotated outward

Assess the pelvis **once**, gently, with a single light inward pressure on the iliac wings. Do not spring it, rock it, or re-test to show your partner. Every repeat compression tears the clot you were trying to build.

## The steps

1. **Expose and clear the area.** Cut clothing away and empty the pockets. A phone, a wallet or a set of keys trapped under a binder produces a pressure ulcer within about an hour.
2. **Get the binder underneath** with minimal movement. Slide it under the knees and work it up toward the hips, or place it on a scoop stretcher, or log-roll once with a full team. One roll only.
3. **Center it over the greater trochanters** — the bony bumps at the top of each femur, roughly level with the pubic symphysis. This is lower than it looks. A binder placed over the **iliac crests is too high** and will not close the ring at all. That single error is the most common mistake made with this device.
4. **Bring the legs in.** Rotate the feet slightly inward and tie the knees and ankles together with cravats or wide tape. Internal rotation closes the ring further.
5. **Tighten until snug**, using the device's own indicator — commercial binders have an audible click, a buckle stop or a marked window. Snug, not crushing: excessive force causes skin necrosis and can over-reduce a lateral compression fracture.
6. **Recheck and document.** Distal pulses, motor and sensation in both legs, and the time of application.
7. **Leave it alone.** Do not remove it to examine the patient, and say clearly at handoff when it went on.

No commercial binder available? A folded sheet `8–10 in` wide, centered over the trochanters, crossed and twisted tight with clamps or tied, does the same job.

> **Trap:** A traction splint is contraindicated in a patient with a pelvic fracture, because traction pulls the ring apart. If the patient has both a femur fracture and a suspected pelvic injury, the binder wins and the femur gets a rigid or vacuum splint.

## Findings that travel with the fracture

Blood at the urethral opening, bruising of the scrotum or perineum, and inability to urinate all suggest urethral injury. Report them; nobody should pass a urinary catheter until that is sorted out. Expect internal bleeding, keep the patient warm, and transport to a trauma center.

> **On the exam:** If the stem says the binder is over the iliac crests, that is the error the question is testing, and the fix is to reposition it down over the greater trochanters.
keyPoints: Most pelvic bleeding is venous and from bone surfaces, so closing the ring reduces volume and lets it tamponade.
A pelvic binder centers over the greater trochanters, not the iliac crests, which is the most common placement error.
Assess the pelvis gently once; repeated compression breaks the clot.
Bind the knees and ankles with the feet rotated slightly inward, tighten to the device indicator, then recheck distal pulses and record the time.
A traction splint is contraindicated with a pelvic fracture; blood at the urethral meatus or perineal bruising suggests urethral injury.

checks.q: You arrive to find a binder already applied over the patient's iliac crests. The patient remains hypotensive. What should you do?
choices: Leave it where it is; repositioning risks further injury
Add a second binder over the first for more pressure
Loosen it and reposition it lower, centered over the greater trochanters
Remove it entirely and use a folded sheet over the abdomen
checks.why: A binder over the iliac crests does not close the pelvic ring and provides no tamponade. Repositioning it down over the greater trochanters, roughly level with the pubic symphysis, is the correction. Stacking binders does not fix the wrong landmark, and a sheet over the abdomen compresses nothing useful.

checks.q: A patient has a suspected pelvic fracture and an isolated closed midshaft femur fracture on the right. Which is correct?
choices: Apply the traction splint first, then the binder
Apply the pelvic binder and splint the femur with a rigid or vacuum splint; no traction
Apply both a traction splint and a binder simultaneously
Apply neither and transport without splinting
checks.why: Traction pulls against the pelvic ring you are trying to close and is contraindicated with a pelvic fracture. The binder controls the larger bleeding source, and the femur is stabilized with a rigid or vacuum splint. Leaving the femur unsplinted allows continued motion and bleeding.

checks.q: Why is it wrong to repeatedly compress the pelvis to test for instability?
choices: It gives falsely negative results after the first attempt
It disrupts the clot that is forming and can restart bleeding
It is painful but otherwise harmless
It can cause the patient to become hypertensive
checks.why: A single gentle assessment is acceptable. Repeat compression moves the fracture surfaces against each other, tears any clot that has formed, and restarts venous bleeding into a space that can hold two liters. It is not merely painful; it actively worsens the injury.

lessons.title: Splints that go wrong: pulseless, open, and dislocated
lessons.body:
## The pulseless angulated limb

A fracture bent far enough can kink or compress the artery running past it. If the limb below is pale, cold, and has no pulse, time matters: muscle tolerates roughly `4–6 hours` of complete ischemia before it dies.

The rule is **one gentle attempt** at realignment, with steady traction applied along the long axis of the limb while a partner supports above the fracture. Pull, do not lever. Stop immediately if you feel firm resistance or the pain spikes sharply, and splint in whatever position you reached. Recheck the pulse, motor and sensation and document all three before and after.

If the limb stays pulseless, say so on the radio. A pulseless extremity changes the receiving team's plan.

## Open fractures

Bone communicating with the outside world means infection is already underway, and the operating room is the treatment. Your job is bleeding control and stabilization.

Control bleeding with direct pressure around, not on, the protruding bone. Cover the exposed bone end with a **moist sterile dressing** so it does not dry. **Do not push it back in.** If realignment for a pulseless limb causes the bone to slide back under the skin on its own, that is acceptable — say so clearly at handoff, because the surgeon needs to know that end was exposed.

## Joints, not bones

A dislocation puts the joint surfaces out of contact, and the vessels and nerves that cross a joint are directly at risk. Splint as found, pad generously, and check circulation, motor and sensation constantly.

**Knee dislocation** is the one to fear. The popliteal artery is tethered behind the knee and is injured in a large minority of true knee dislocations. Even a knee that looks like it relocated itself can have a torn artery. Pulseless knee dislocation is a limb-threatening surgical emergency, so check the foot pulse, check it again, and call it in.

**Posterior hip dislocation** typically comes from a knee striking the dashboard. The leg is shortened, turned inward and pulled toward the midline, and the sciatic nerve runs right there — ask about foot numbness and foot drop. Support the leg in the position found with pillows and rolled blankets.

**Anterior shoulder dislocation** holds the arm slightly out from the body and rotated outward, and the patient physically cannot bring the elbow to the ribs. A standard sling and swathe will not fit. Pad the gap between arm and chest and immobilize where it sits.

**Ankle fracture-dislocation** with white, tented, blanched skin over a bone end is the one case where many protocols permit a gentle field reduction, because that skin will die before the patient reaches an operating room. Follow your protocol and call medical direction.

> **Key:** Splint it as found. The two exceptions are a limb with no distal pulse and skin about to break over a deformity, and both get one careful attempt.

## Hands, fingers, and rings

Remove rings, watches and bracelets at the first opportunity — before swelling turns them into tourniquets. Buddy-tape an injured finger to its neighbor with padding between. Keep the hand in the position of function: a slight cup, as if holding a small ball, achieved with a roll of gauze in the palm.

A **degloving** injury, where skin is stripped off like a glove, is a surgical emergency; keep the skin with the patient, cover with moist sterile dressings, and go.

## Sequencing an unstable patient

A patient who is unstable does not get individually splinted on scene. Secure the whole patient to a rigid device — a scoop or vacuum mattress splints everything at once — and move. Do splinting en route if you have hands free, or not at all.

> **On shift:** The two documentation questions that follow every extremity injury are whether you checked pulses before and after the splint, and what time a tourniquet or binder went on. Write them the moment you do them.
keyPoints: A pulseless angulated limb gets one gentle attempt at realignment with axial traction; stop for resistance and splint where you reached.
Cover exposed bone with a moist sterile dressing, never push it back in, and report it if realignment pulls it under the skin.
Knee dislocation threatens the popliteal artery even after apparent relocation, so recheck the foot pulse repeatedly.
Posterior hip dislocation leaves the leg shortened, internally rotated and adducted, with the sciatic nerve at risk.
Remove rings early, keep the hand in the position of function, and splint an unstable patient as a whole rather than limb by limb.

checks.q: A forearm fracture is grossly angulated and the hand below it is cold, pale and pulseless. What is the correct action?
choices: Splint exactly as found and transport without moving it
Apply a tourniquet above the fracture to control unseen bleeding
Make one gentle attempt at realignment with traction along the limb axis, then splint and recheck the pulse
Make repeated attempts until a pulse returns
checks.why: Absent distal circulation is the one indication to move an angulated fracture. One careful attempt with axial traction may free the vessel. Repeated attempts cause more damage, a tourniquet on a limb that is already ischemic is harmful, and splinting as found guarantees the limb stays without blood flow.

checks.q: A patient dislocated his knee in a fall, and it appears to have relocated on its own. Distal pulses are present. What is the correct concern?
choices: None; a relocated knee with pulses is a minor injury
The popliteal artery may still be injured, so recheck pulses frequently and notify the receiving facility
The main risk is a torn meniscus requiring outpatient follow-up
It should be re-dislocated to relieve pressure on the nerve
checks.why: Knee dislocations injure the popliteal artery in a large minority of cases, and the artery can be torn or thrombosing while a pulse is still present. Serial pulse checks and early notification are the standard. A meniscus tear is not the emergency, and deliberately re-dislocating a joint is never correct.

checks.q: You realign a pulseless open tibia fracture and the protruding bone end slips back beneath the skin. What should you do?
choices: Reopen the wound so the surgeon can see the bone
Document that the bone was exposed and report it clearly at handoff
Say nothing, since the wound is now closed
Apply a tourniquet because the fracture is now internally displaced
checks.why: Bone retracting during a justified realignment attempt is acceptable, but the wound is still contaminated and the fracture is still open. The surgical team needs to know so antibiotics and washout are not delayed. Reopening a wound is harmful, and staying quiet changes the patient's treatment for the worse.

lessons.title: Athletes, helmets, and equipment removal
lessons.body:
## The spine-injured athlete is a different problem

Sports spinal injuries come from axial loading: a head-down tackle, a hockey player driven into the boards, a diver hitting the bottom, a gymnast landing on the neck. The force runs straight down the cervical spine and the neck buckles.

What makes an athlete different is the equipment. A helmet and shoulder pads together hold the head and torso in a reasonable position relative to each other. Take one off and the head drops or rises relative to the shoulders, and the neck moves. That is the entire logic of equipment management.

> **Key:** Helmet and shoulder pads come off **together, or neither comes off**. Removing just the helmet extends the neck; removing just the pads flexes it.

## Leave it on, take it off

**Leave the helmet in place** when it fits snugly, the head does not move inside it, the airway and breathing are adequate or reachable, and the face can be accessed.

**Remove it** when it blocks airway management or ventilation you cannot otherwise provide, when the head moves freely inside it, when it prevents holding the spine in a neutral position, or when the patient is in cardiac arrest.

For football and lacrosse the preferred first move is **not** removal — it is removing the **face mask**. Cutting or unscrewing the clips that hold the mask frees the entire airway while the helmet and its padding keep the head where it is. Carry a cordless screwdriver and a mask-cutting tool; screws strip and corrode, so a cutter is the backup, not the plan.

Hockey helmets often have a cage that unclips or a shield that lifts. Baseball and softball catchers' masks lift straight off.

## How removal is done

It takes two providers minimum and is a slow, deliberate maneuver.

1. Provider one takes manual in-line stabilization from **below**, hands on the jaw angles and the occiput, reaching under the helmet edge.
2. Provider two removes the chin strap, then **spreads the shell laterally** to clear the ears and lifts it off in a straight line, tilting slightly to clear the nose if needed.
3. Provider one maintains stabilization the whole time, adjusting hand position as the helmet comes away.
4. Reassess the airway, then pad appropriately: with the pads still on, the head needs support behind it; with everything off, an adult usually needs padding behind the head to stay neutral.

Full-face motorcycle helmets are the hardest because the chin bar traps the nose. Take the eye protection out first if it comes free.

## Working a field

Work with the athletic trainer. They know the equipment, they saw the mechanism, and they often have the right tools already in hand. An **eight-person lift** — several providers lifting the athlete straight up while one controls the head — moves an equipped athlete onto a board or scoop with less motion than a log roll.

A **prone athlete** who is unresponsive must be turned to supine as a unit, with the provider at the head starting with crossed arms so their hands unwind into the correct position as the body rolls.

## Burners, stingers, and the scary ones

A **burner or stinger** is a brachial plexus stretch: burning pain and weakness down **one** arm, resolving within minutes. It is not a cord injury, but the athlete still gets examined.

**Transient quadriplegia** is different — burning, numbness or weakness in **all four limbs** after a blow, often resolving within minutes to hours. Resolution does not make it benign. That athlete is immobilized and transported.

Any athlete with neck pain, midline tenderness, any neurologic symptom, or an altered level of consciousness gets full spinal motion restriction on the field, equipment and all.

> **Trap:** Do not let a coach, a parent, or the athlete talk you out of restriction because the symptoms resolved on the sideline. Transient symptoms after axial loading are a reason to go, not a reason to stay.
keyPoints: Helmet and shoulder pads come off together or neither comes off, because removing one alone angles the neck.
For football and lacrosse, remove the face mask first; the helmet and its padding stay and hold the head in place.
Remove a helmet when it blocks airway management, when the head moves inside it, or when the patient is in arrest.
Helmet removal takes two providers, with stabilization applied from below while the shell is spread laterally and lifted straight off.
A stinger affects one arm and resolves; symptoms in all four limbs after axial loading mean immobilize and transport even if they resolve.

checks.q: A football player is down with neck pain after a head-down tackle. He is breathing adequately but you want airway access available. What is the preferred first step?
choices: Remove the helmet, leaving the shoulder pads in place
Remove the face mask, leaving the helmet and shoulder pads in place
Remove the shoulder pads, leaving the helmet in place
Remove both helmet and pads immediately
checks.why: Face mask removal opens the entire airway while the helmet and pads continue to hold the head and torso in their proper relationship. Removing the helmet alone extends the neck; removing the pads alone flexes it. Taking everything off is reserved for situations where the equipment actually blocks care.

checks.q: A wrestler took a hard blow and had burning and weakness in all four limbs for about two minutes, and now feels completely normal. What is the correct management?
choices: Clear him to return once symptoms have resolved
Have him sit out the match and follow up with his own doctor
Immobilize and transport, because four-limb symptoms after axial loading suggest transient quadriplegia
Check grip strength and release him if it is equal
checks.why: Symptoms in all four limbs point to the cord, not a peripheral nerve, and transient quadriplegia can be associated with an unstable injury or with cervical stenosis. Resolution does not clear him. A stinger, by contrast, affects one arm only, and even that athlete is examined.

checks.q: During helmet removal, where does the provider maintaining in-line stabilization place their hands?
choices: On the outside of the helmet shell at the temples
Under the helmet edge, on the angles of the jaw and the occiput, from below
On the forehead and chin over the face mask
Across the shoulders to control the torso
checks.why: The person holding the head must have direct contact with the patient, not the helmet, because the helmet is the thing being removed. Reaching under the shell to hold the jaw angles and occiput keeps the head still while the second provider spreads and lifts the shell away.

lessons.title: Face and Neck Injuries
lessons.body:
## Why the face and neck scare you first

The face sits directly in front of the airway, and the neck holds the airway, the great vessels, and the spinal cord in a space you can wrap two hands around. A hurt face or neck is rarely the worst injury on the patient, but it is often the one that kills fastest. **Manage the airway threat before you catalog the wound.**

## Facial fractures

Blunt force to the face — a steering wheel, a fist, a fall — can fracture the bones around the eyes, nose, cheek, and jaw. Swelling, bruising, deformity, and a bite that no longer lines up (malocclusion) suggest a fracture. The danger is not the bone, it is what the bone carries with it: blood, broken teeth, dentures, and swelling tissue that drop into the airway the patient is trying to breathe through. **Any facial trauma is an airway problem until proven otherwise** — have suction ready and reassess often.

A midface fracture pattern called **LeFort** (I, II, III, by how high the break runs) can leave the entire midface mobile, moving as one unstable segment. You will not classify the level in the field; the point to carry is that a mobile midface is a major airway threat. A **mandible fracture** lets the tongue lose its anchor and fall backward into the airway when supine — a conscious patient often protects their own airway best sitting up and leaning forward, if spinal precautions allow it.

> **Trap:** A calm, talking patient with facial injury can go from stable to obstructed in minutes as swelling progresses. Reassess.

## Teeth, eyes, ears, and nose

A knocked-out (avulsed) tooth is a save if you handle it right. Pick it up by the crown, never the root — touching the root kills the cells that let it reattach. Rinse gently if dirty. Store it in cold milk or saline; reimplantation odds drop fast after about `30–60` minutes.

Eye injuries follow firm rules. An **impaled object stays in place** — stabilize it and shield both eyes, since the uninjured eye moves with the injured one. **Chemical burns get a continuous flush for at least 20 minutes**, before you worry about which chemical it was. **Hyphema** is blood pooling in front of the iris; keep the patient sitting up. A **ruptured globe** gets a rigid shield resting only on the bony orbit, never pressure on the eye. Cover both eyes in any serious eye injury.

Ear and nose injuries bleed dramatically but are rarely life-threatening alone. For a nosebleed, sit the patient forward and pinch the soft part of the nose for `10–15` minutes. Clear or blood-tinged fluid from the nose or ear after head trauma can be cerebrospinal fluid signaling a skull fracture — do not pack it.

## The neck: small space, everything that matters

An open neck wound is a two-part emergency: it can bleed fast from a major vessel, and an open vein near the heart can pull air in with each breath (air embolism), which can stop the heart. Seal it with an **occlusive dressing** taped on all four sides plus direct pressure. Never wrap circumferentially around the neck; it can compress the airway or the opposite vessel.

Blunt neck trauma — a clothesline mechanism, a strike across the throat — can fracture the larynx or trachea with no visible wound. Watch for **subcutaneous emphysema** (a crackling feel under the skin), voice change, stridor, or bruising across the throat — any of these means the airway may be failing and can close progressively; treat as load-and-go. An **expanding hematoma** in the neck is compressing the airway and vessels in real time and is one of the clearest do-not-wait findings in trauma.

> **Key:** Neck trauma with stridor, voice change, or subcutaneous emphysema means the airway is failing from the inside — this patient needs rapid transport to definitive airway care.

## Spinal precautions and the NPA exception

Significant facial or neck trauma often comes from a mechanism that can also injure the cervical spine, so maintain spinal precautions while managing the airway — the two happen together. Reconsider the **nasopharyngeal airway (NPA)** here: it is relatively contraindicated with significant midface or basilar skull trauma, because of a rare but real risk of passing it through a fracture into the cranial vault. Clear nasal fluid, raccoon eyes, or Battle's sign are reasons to reach for an oropharyngeal airway instead.
keyPoints: Any facial trauma is an airway problem first — blood, teeth, and swelling all drop into the same airway; have suction ready and reassess often.
Avulsed teeth: handle by the crown only, rinse gently if dirty, store in cold milk or saline, reimplantation odds drop fast after 30–60 minutes.
Impaled eye objects stay in place and get shielded; chemical burns get 20+ minutes of continuous flush; ruptured globe gets a rigid shield with no pressure; cover both eyes.
Open neck wounds need an occlusive dressing taped on all four sides (air embolism risk) plus direct pressure — never a circumferential wrap.

Subcutaneous emphysema, voice change, stridor, or an expanding hematoma after neck trauma mean the airway is failing internally, and NPA is relatively contraindicated with midface or basilar skull trauma.

checks.q: A patient has significant blunt facial trauma with an unstable, mobile midface. Beyond the visible injury, what is the primary concern?
choices: Cosmetic deformity requiring early surgical consult
The airway, since blood, teeth, and swelling from the injury can obstruct it quickly
Hearing loss from associated ear trauma
Delayed capillary refill in the extremities
checks.why: A mobile midface signals high-energy trauma and a direct threat to the airway from bleeding, avulsed teeth, and progressive swelling. Cosmetic and hearing concerns are real but are not the immediate life threat; distal perfusion isn't the mechanism at play in facial injury.

checks.q: You find an avulsed permanent tooth at a scene. What is the correct handling?
choices: Scrub the root clean under tap water, then wrap it dry in gauze
Pick it up by the crown, rinse gently if dirty, and store it in cold milk or saline
Soak it in rubbing alcohol to prevent infection before transport
Reinsert it into the socket immediately regardless of contamination
checks.why: Handling by the crown protects the root's cell layer, which is what allows reimplantation to succeed; milk or saline preserves those cells, tap water and dry storage kill them, and scrubbing the root destroys the same tissue you're trying to save. Reimplantation is time sensitive but not appropriate to force onto a dirty, unassessed socket in the field without direction.

checks.q: A patient has a ruptured globe after blunt eye trauma. What is the correct field management?
choices: Apply a firmly wrapped pressure dressing directly over the eye
Irrigate the eye continuously for 20 minutes
Place a rigid shield resting on the bony orbit, touching only bone, and cover both eyes
Attempt to gently reposition any extruded contents before covering
checks.why: A rigid shield that bears on the orbital bone protects the globe without adding pressure, which could push more contents out; covering both eyes prevents the sympathetic eye movement that worsens the injury. Pressure dressings and repositioning contents can cause further extrusion, and irrigation is the chemical-burn protocol, not the ruptured-globe one.

cards.front: Why do children more often have multisystem injury than adults from the same force?
cards.back: The same kinetic energy spreads across a smaller body with less fat and muscle and organs packed closer together, so it reaches several systems at once instead of being absorbed by one.

cards.front: A child from a crash has no rib fractures on the initial exam. What does that rule out?
cards.back: Nothing. Pediatric ribs are partly cartilage and bend rather than break, so severe pulmonary contusion occurs behind a normal chest wall. Rib fractures in a small child mean enormous force.

cards.front: Why do you pad under a small child's shoulders and torso during immobilization?
cards.back: The occiput is proportionally huge, so lying flat pushes the neck into flexion and narrows the airway. Padding from shoulders to hips raises the body to match the head and restores neutral alignment.

cards.front: What is the formula for the systolic blood pressure floor in a child past age 1?
cards.back: Roughly `70 + (2 x age in years)`. A 4-year-old floors at about 78, a 10-year-old at about 90. Below that number the child is hypotensive.

cards.front: How much blood volume has a child lost by the time they become hypotensive?
cards.back: About 30 to 45 percent. Children clamp down hard and hold pressure until reserves are gone, so hypotension in a child is a near-arrest finding.

cards.front: What is a child's total blood volume per kilogram, and why does it matter?
cards.back: About 70 to 80 mL/kg, so a 20 kg child holds roughly 1.5 liters. Scalp lacerations and small losses that are trivial in adults become class II hemorrhage in a child.

cards.front: What are the three sides of the pediatric assessment triangle?
cards.back: Appearance, work of breathing, and circulation to skin, all judged from the doorway before touching the child. A child who will not cry, look at you, or fight the exam is sick.

cards.front: Which findings raise concern for inflicted injury in a child?
cards.back: Injury that does not match the story, a changing story, delayed call, bruising to torso, ears or neck under age 4, any bruise on a non-cruising infant, patterned burns, and infant rib fractures.

cards.front: Why may an older trauma patient in shock have a normal heart rate?
cards.back: Maximum heart rate falls with age, and beta blockers or rate-controlling calcium channel blockers prevent the compensatory tachycardia entirely. The absence of tachycardia does not exclude shock.

cards.front: An 82-year-old trauma patient has a blood pressure of 118/70. Why might that be alarming?
cards.back: Stiff arteries raise baseline pressure with age. If he normally lives at 170/90, he has lost roughly a third of his usual pressure while the number still reads as textbook normal.

cards.front: Why do older adults develop subdural hematomas after trivial mechanisms?
cards.back: The brain shrinks with age, stretching the bridging veins that tear easily, and the extra space lets blood accumulate before any pressure sign appears. Symptoms can take days to weeks.

cards.front: What is central cord syndrome and how does it happen?
cards.back: A hyperextension injury, often a fall onto the face in an arthritic neck, that causes weakness worse in the hands and arms than the legs, often with burning pain, frequently with no fracture at all.

cards.front: Why are rib fractures a bigger deal in a patient over 65?
cards.back: Each additional fractured rib raises mortality and pneumonia risk, because pain causes shallow breathing, alveolar collapse and infection. Three or more rib fractures in an older adult warrants a trauma center.

cards.front: Name the reversal agents for warfarin, dabigatran, and apixaban.
cards.back: Warfarin: vitamin K plus clotting factor concentrate. Dabigatran: idarucizumab. Apixaban and rivaroxaban: andexanet alfa or factor concentrate. Antiplatelets such as clopidogrel have no true reversal agent.

cards.front: An older patient on apixaban bumped her head and has a normal exam. What is the disposition?
cards.back: Transport for imaging and usually observation. Bleeding on anticoagulants can be delayed by hours, and anticoagulant use with head injury is a field triage consideration for a trauma center.

cards.front: How do you immobilize a patient whose kyphosis prevents her head from reaching the stretcher?
cards.back: Fill the gap with padding and secure her in her existing curve. Never press the head down to flat; forcing a fused spine straight can injure the cord. Use towel rolls if no collar fits.

cards.front: How much blood can a third-trimester patient lose before her vital signs change?
cards.back: About 1200 to 1500 mL. Blood volume rises 40 to 50 percent and the heart rate runs 10 to 20 beats faster at baseline, so the usual warning signs are blunted.

cards.front: Why does fetal distress appear before maternal vital signs change?
cards.back: The mother's body defends her core by shunting blood away from the uterus first. The placenta is sacrificed early, so normal maternal numbers say nothing about the fetus.

cards.front: What is supine hypotensive syndrome and how do you fix it?
cards.back: After about 20 weeks the uterus compresses the vena cava when she lies flat, dropping cardiac output by up to 30 percent. Tilt the board 15 to 30 degrees left, or manually displace the uterus left.

cards.front: How do you estimate gestational age from fundal height?
cards.back: At the pubic symphysis is about 12 weeks, at the umbilicus about 20 weeks, and roughly 1 cm above the symphysis per week after that. Twenty weeks is the threshold for left tilt.

cards.front: What is placental abruption and what are its signs?
cards.back: The placenta shearing off the uterine wall after deceleration. Abdominal pain, a firm rigid tender uterus, contractions, and bleeding that is frequently concealed behind the placenta. It is the leading cause of fetal death in a surviving mother.

cards.front: Why does a pregnant patient past 20 weeks go to the hospital even after a minor crash?
cards.back: Abruption can be concealed, can follow low-speed mechanisms, and can declare itself hours later. Standard care is transport plus 4 to 6 hours of fetal heart and contraction monitoring.

cards.front: Where does a seat belt belong on a pregnant patient?
cards.back: The lap belt low across the hips and under the belly, with the shoulder belt between the breasts and off to the side of the uterus. A belt across the uterus transmits force to the placenta.

cards.front: How is CPR modified for a pregnant patient past 20 weeks?
cards.back: Continuous manual left uterine displacement throughout, with standard hand position on the lower half of the sternum. The hospital target for resuscitative hysterotomy is about 4 to 5 minutes into the arrest.

cards.front: Why does an odd number of holes matter in a gunshot patient?
cards.back: Wounds come in entrance and exit pairs when the round passes through. An odd count means something is still inside, so expose fully and search the back, axilla, groin, perineum and scalp.

cards.front: What is the cardiac box and why does it matter?
cards.back: The rectangle between the nipples, from the sternal notch to the costal margin. Penetrating wounds there threaten the heart and great vessels, so cardiac tamponade belongs on your list immediately.

cards.front: Where is the thoracoabdominal zone and why is it dangerous?
cards.back: From the nipple line in front and the scapular tip in back down to the costal margins. The diaphragm rises to the fourth intercostal space on exhalation, so wounds there can be chest and abdominal injuries at once.

cards.front: Name the three zones of the neck.
cards.back: Zone I from the clavicles to the cricoid cartilage, zone II from the cricoid to the angle of the jaw, and zone III from the angle of the jaw to the skull base. Zone II is the most commonly injured.

cards.front: List the hard signs of vascular injury in a penetrating wound.
cards.back: Expanding or pulsatile hematoma, severe active bleeding, bruit or thrill, absent or diminished distal pulse, airway compromise or an enlarging neck, and massive hemoptysis or hematemesis.

cards.front: How do you dress an open wound to the neck, and what must you avoid?
cards.back: Occlusive dressing to prevent air embolism, with direct pressure over the vessel. Never wrap circumferentially around the neck and never compress both sides at once.

cards.front: What spinal care applies to isolated penetrating trauma with no neurologic deficit?
cards.back: None. Routine motion restriction delays surgery, hides expanding hematomas, and is associated with worse outcomes. Restrict only if there is a neurologic deficit.

cards.front: What scene details should you collect for a penetrating trauma handoff?
cards.back: Weapon type and caliber if known, number of shots heard, distance from the shooter, blade length and angle for stabbings, time of injury, and whether the patient walked or was carried.

cards.front: What do crushed muscle cells release, and where does it go while the weight is on?
cards.back: Potassium, phosphate, myoglobin, uric acid and lactic acid. While the weight remains, it stays trapped locally, which is why the patient can look well during entrapment.

cards.front: What four problems arrive at the moment a crush is released?
cards.back: Hyperkalemia causing lethal rhythms, myoglobin causing acute kidney injury, metabolic acidosis, and hypocalcemia as calcium is drawn into damaged muscle. Hypovolemia is already present from third spacing.

cards.front: What is the ECG progression of rising potassium after a crush release?
cards.back: Peaked T waves, then a widening QRS, then a sine-wave pattern, then ventricular fibrillation or asystole. It can happen within minutes of the load coming off.

cards.front: What should happen before a crushed patient is freed?
cards.back: ALS on scene, cardiac monitor applied, vascular access with isotonic fluid running before release, and potassium-shifting drugs available. The EMT calls early, notes the entrapment start time and keeps the patient warm.

cards.front: How much fluid can a badly crushed limb third-space, and over what period?
cards.back: Up to 10 to 12 liters over about 48 hours. That fluid leaves the circulation, so the patient is already hypovolemic before the object is lifted.

cards.front: At what overpressure do eardrums rupture, and can you use that to screen for blast lung?
cards.back: Around 5 psi. No. Eardrum rupture is neither sensitive nor specific for blast lung, so an intact eardrum does not reassure and a ruptured one does not diagnose.

cards.front: Why is a blast inside a building or underwater worse than the same device outdoors?
cards.back: The pressure wave reflects off surfaces instead of dissipating, multiplying the overpressure. The same charge that bruises someone in a parking lot can cause fatal blast lung in a bus or a room.

cards.front: A blast patient deteriorates right after you begin bag-valve-mask ventilation. What should you think?
cards.back: Tension pneumothorax or arterial gas embolism. Damaged lung tears under positive pressure and air can be forced into torn vessels. Use high-flow oxygen and ventilate gently.

cards.front: How long is a tourniquet routinely safe, and what is the longest limbs have survived?
cards.back: About 2 hours routinely. Limbs have been salvaged after roughly 6 hours on a properly applied device. Tourniquet-caused limb loss is rare; the bleeding is what kills.

cards.front: Should a tourniquet be loosened periodically to let blood back into the limb?
cards.back: Never. Intermittent release restarts bleeding and repeatedly washes potassium and acid into the circulation. Once it is on and tight, it stays until a hospital or a protocol-driven conversion removes it.

cards.front: Why are belts, cords and wire poor improvised tourniquets?
cards.back: They are narrow and hard to tension. They often occlude veins without stopping arterial inflow, which increases bleeding, and the narrow band crushes tissue. A strap at least 1.5 inches wide is needed.
